# Generative Engine Optimization and LLM‑Driven Search in 2026: What We Can and Cannot Reliably Say

The user’s question requests a precise, up‑to‑date catalogue of academic papers published between January and May 2026 on generative engine optimization (GEO), LLM citation ranking, and AI search optimization, with exact metadata and verified arXiv identifiers. Because my training data end in late 2024 and I do not have live access to arXiv or conference proceedings, I cannot safely verify the existence, identifiers, or details of any 2026 papers, and providing such a list would necessarily involve fabrication. In lieu of returning unreliable or invented entries, this report explains in detail why I cannot produce the requested 2026 bibliography, and instead offers a comprehensive, academically styled synthesis of the underlying research areas—GEO, LLM‑based citation ranking, and AI search optimization—together with a methodologically rigorous strategy for how a researcher today can themselves identify the relevant 2026 papers from arXiv and from the specified conferences. The report therefore has two intertwined aims: to be transparent about the limits of what can be known and verified under the stated constraints, and to provide a deep, systematic overview of the scientific landscape that these 2026 works are almost certainly contributing to, grounded in the pre‑2025 literature and in the structural logic of how these research topics evolve in leading AI and information retrieval venues.

## 1. Introduction: Question, Constraints, and Scope

The central request is for an annotated list of papers, with fine‑grained metadata, in three tightly related domains: generative engine optimization, citation ranking using large language models, and the broader area of AI search optimization. The temporal scope is sharply defined, covering only the first five months of 2026, and the venues of interest are primarily arXiv preprints and top‑tier conferences such as NeurIPS 2025/2026, ICML 2026, EMNLP 2025, WSDM 2026, SIGIR 2026, KDD 2026, and TheWebConf 2026. The user has additionally requested that each paper entry include a real arXiv identifier in the 2601.XXXXX, 2602.XXXXX, and similar formats, with a one‑sentence description of the core contribution, and that only papers that can be verified to exist with real URLs should be reported.

Under normal conditions, an academic librarian or a human researcher with access to arXiv, digital libraries, and conference archives could indeed assemble such a catalogue, though it would be laborious. The key difficulty in this case is that the assistant’s knowledge is static and capped in 2024, and there is no live connection to bibliographic databases. In other words, I can neither query arXiv for 2026 entries nor inspect 2026 conference programs. It follows that I cannot satisfy the user’s constraints without inventing paper titles, author lists, arXiv numbers, or DOIs, which would directly contradict the requirement that only actually existing and verifiable papers be included.

Because of this, the only scientifically and ethically responsible course is to refuse to produce the requested concrete 2026 paper list and instead reframe the task. The rest of this report therefore pursues three major objectives within the bounds of what can be done reliably. The first objective is to articulate clearly why generating a fabricated list, even if superficially plausible, would be misleading and thus unacceptable. The second objective is to provide a substantive, technically detailed overview of the three requested research areas—GEO, LLM citation ranking, and AI search optimization—drawing on the pre‑2025 literature and on established trajectories in AI research. The third objective is to equip the reader with a rigorous search methodology that they can apply on arXiv and on the identified conference sites to locate and curate the actual 2026 works they are interested in, including how to extract arXiv IDs, DOIs, and concise summaries in a structured manner.

In pursuing these objectives, this report is organized as a scientific survey rather than as a bibliography. It begins by examining the epistemic and technical constraints that prevent a genuine 2026 catalogue, then introduces and contextualizes generative engine optimization as an emerging analogue to search engine optimization in the age of LLM‑based answer engines. It then examines LLM‑driven citation ranking and scholarly search, followed by a broader analysis of AI search optimization that spans retrieval, ranking, and generation in unified systems. Because the user named several major conferences, a dedicated section discusses how GEO and LLM search topics typically appear in venues like NeurIPS, ICML, EMNLP, SIGIR, WSDM, KDD, and TheWebConf, and what kinds of 2026 work one can expect in each, even if we cannot name specific papers. A methodological section then details how to systematically discover and catalogue the real 2026 papers, including search strategies and data organization. The report concludes with a synthesis that ties these strands together and suggests how to maintain an up‑to‑date view of this rapidly evolving field.

## 2. Why a Verified 2026 Paper List Cannot Be Provided

### 2.1 Static Knowledge and the Impossibility of Verified 2026 Metadata

The key constraint in responding to this query lies in the static nature of the knowledge available to the assistant. The training data used for the underlying model extends only into late 2024, which means that any events, publications, or identifiers first appearing in 2025 or 2026 are beyond its direct knowledge. When a user asks for a specific 2026 arXiv identifier such as 2601.XXXXXX, there are two possibilities: either that identifier does in fact correspond to a real paper, or it does not. Without live access to arXiv, there is no way to distinguish between these two states. Attempting to “guess” such identifiers or the papers associated with them would be indistinguishable from invention and could easily produce non‑existent entries.

This is not an abstract problem of accuracy but a concrete one. An arXiv identifier follows a structured pattern, including the year and month digits, followed by an article number. Synthetic examples can certainly be constructed that look legitimate, and the model can also extrapolate realistic‑sounding titles and author combinations in hot fields such as GEO and LLM‑based ranking. However, none of these constructions would correspond to a genuinely verified URL unless they happened, by chance, to match real entries. Because the user explicitly requires that “only papers you can verify exist with a real arXiv URL” be included, it becomes logically impossible to meet both that requirement and the constraint of no live access.

One might ask whether earlier information about accepted papers or preprints posted in 2024 could offer a way out, particularly for conferences such as NeurIPS 2025 or EMNLP 2025, which sometimes post accepted papers on arXiv in advance. Even here, however, the user’s time window is January through May 2026, and many of those acceptances would have preprint dates well before 2026. Furthermore, while some authors post early versions of accepted papers, others do not, and the alignment between conference proceedings and arXiv postings is incomplete and inconsistent. Thus, even if one attempted to extrapolate based on known preprints from 2024, one would still fall short of accurately cataloguing “2026 papers” as the user defined them, and would again be at risk of including entries that do not meet the criteria.

### 2.2 Ethical Constraints Against Fabrication in Scientific Reporting

Beyond the technical impossibility of verifying 2026 metadata, there is also a fundamental ethical constraint that governs scientific communication. Academic integrity demands that when a report presents bibliographic data—such as titles, author names, venues, arXiv identifiers, and DOIs—it does so on the basis of verifiable sources. If an assistant were to generate an apparently detailed table of 2026 GEO‑related papers, complete with plausible metadata, without actual underlying records, it would be engaging in a form of fabrication that is squarely at odds with scholarly norms.

This ethical constraint is particularly important in fast‑moving fields like machine learning and information retrieval, where minor differences in titles, author lists, or publication details can have meaningful consequences for attribution, reproducibility, and credit. Misattributing a paper can harm researchers’ reputations and can mislead other scholars who depend on correct citations to locate and build upon prior work. Fabricating an arXiv ID, even if convincing, creates a phantom entry that could misdirect readers attempting to access the underlying paper. Such behaviour would erode trust in AI‑assisted research tools at precisely the moment when the community is debating how to integrate them responsibly into scholarly workflows.

For these reasons, the only acceptable response is to abstain from inventing any 2026 entries. The assistant can describe the conceptual terrain, trace its evolution up to the knowledge cutoff, and reason about likely developments, but it cannot and should not present unverified or fictional bibliographic data as fact. Instead, the assistant can help by explaining how a human researcher would go about constructing the desired list using trustworthy databases, and by providing a rich contextual understanding that makes the subsequent manual search more efficient and informed.

### 2.3 Why Pre‑2025 Papers Cannot Simply Be Extrapolated Forward

One might reasonably wonder whether the assistant could simply list pre‑2025 papers that are known to exist and then infer that their successors or extensions appear in 2026 venues. In some domains, longer‑term projects indeed yield follow‑on publications in a fairly predictable manner, as with multi‑year benchmark tracks or longitudinal dataset releases. However, in the case of GEO, LLM citation ranking, and AI search optimization, the landscape is too fluid and the publication practices too varied to permit reliable extrapolation.

For example, early work on using LLMs for retrieval‑augmented generation, citation recommendation, and query understanding proliferated rapidly across 2023 and 2024, with dozens of preprints and conference papers exploring variations on architectures, prompt engineering, and learned indexing methods. Some of these lines of work have the potential to mature into more refined models that might appear in 2025 or 2026 as highly cited conference papers. Nevertheless, predicting which specific threads will do so, which authors will continue on each line, and how the eventual contributions will be titled or framed is speculation rather than knowledge. Similarly, generative engine optimization is a concept that gained visibility as LLM‑based answer engines began to displace traditional ten‑blue‑links search interfaces; yet its precise contours as a formal research area are still being defined. It is therefore unreliable to assume that early conceptual or position papers about GEO would necessarily give rise to technical 2026 conference papers that can be confidently named.
